concepts.title: Nature and Classification of Manufacturing
concepts.definition: Secondary activities transform raw materials into finished goods; manufacturing is classified by scale (artisan, craft, cottage, factory, large-scale), by raw material (agro-based, mineral-based, forest-based) and by ownership (public, private, joint, multinational).
concepts.key_idea: Value addition is the test of manufacturing: the product must be worth more than the raw materials and labour that entered it.
question_patterns: define manufacturing and value addition
classify industries by scale of production
differentiate cottage from factory industry
give examples of agro-based and mineral-based industries
how does ownership distinguish public and joint sector units

solution_steps.explain: changing cotton cloth to garments raises worth, the definition of manufacturing
scale, raw material and ownership are three independent classification axes
steel from ore and sugar from cane show mineral and agro bases

concepts.title: Location Factors of Industry
concepts.definition: Industrial location is decided by access to raw materials, market, labour, power, transport and capital, moderated by agglomeration economies and government policy; modern footloose and high-tech industries escape the raw material pull and follow skilled labour and communication networks.
concepts.key_idea: When raw material is weight-losing the factory moves to the source; when the product is perishable or heavy it moves to the market.
concepts.textbook_ref: legy105.txt location factors and footloose industry sections
question_patterns: list the major factors of industrial location
why do weight-losing industries locate near raw materials
what are agglomeration economies

solution_steps.explain: raw material, market, labour, power and transport anchor classical location theory
sugar and copper smelting move to sources because weight is lost in processing
software firms follow skilled minds and data links, not mines

concepts.title: Major Manufacturing Regions
concepts.definition: Modern manufacturing is highly concentrated: the major manufacturing regions of North America, Europe and East Asia cover less than 10 per cent of the world's land area, so the remaining land share is about 90 per cent outside these belts.
concepts.key_idea: Subtracting the manufacturing belt share from 100 gives the land share outside the great manufacturing regions.

solution_steps.explain: the belts cover about 10 per cent of land
the remainder lies outside the belts

concepts.title: Theories of Industrial Location
concepts.definition: Location theory explains the best site for a plant: Weber's least-cost approach minimises transport and labour costs through locational triangles, while modern thinking adds agglomeration, government policy and innovation networks to the calculus.
concepts.key_idea: Weighing transport against labour and agglomeration costs is the durable core of industrial location reasoning.
concepts.textbook_ref: legy105.txt least-cost theory and agglomeration discussions
question_patterns: state Weber's least-cost theory and its locational triangle

compare classical and modern location thinking

solution_steps.explain: two material sources and one market set Weber's minimum-cost geometry
cheap labour or clustered services can pull the plant off the pure transport point
policy zones and innovation districts reshape the classic map today

worked_examples.question_pattern: Major manufacturing regions cover about 10 per cent of the world's land. Compute the land share outside these regions.

solution_template.explain: 10 per cent of land lies under manufacturing belts

worked_examples.question_pattern: Why does a sugar mill locate near cane fields while a garment factory may locate in a city?

solution_template.explain: cane loses most of its weight in milling, so transport favours the field site
garments gain value per unit weight and need urban labour and fashion information
the weight-to-value ratio decides the pull of source versus market

worked_examples.question_pattern: List three features that make a high-tech industry footloose.

solution_template.explain: chips and software carry little weight per rupee of value
researchers matter more than ore or cheap power
data highways replace rail links as the vital connection
